title: Italy approves elections overhaul as opposition accuse Meloni of 'scam' law
description: Italy's parliament has approved fiercely contested changes to the country's electoral system championed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni ahead of elec
body: Italy's parliament has approved fiercely contested changes to the country's electoral system championed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni ahead of elections due next year.Lawmakers voted 227 to 164 in favour of moving to a fully proportional system, which Meloni has argued will boost the chance of clear winners and more stable government.Opposition parties say her right-wing coalition has designed the proposals to improve its chance of retaining power and, in a heated debate on Thursday, accused it of pushing through the "fraudulent" reform to flout democracy.Meloni had warned she could resign and trigger an early election if the plans were rejected, with the secret ballot seen as a test of her authority.Meloni's coalition has overseen a rare period of political stability for Italy since her election in 2022, and last month her government became the country's longest-running since World War Two.The voting reform will see the country move away from its current hybrid voting system, in which about a third of members are chosen through a first-past-the-post vote and the rest through proportional representation.Parties proposing to form a coalition will be required to put forward their joint candidate for prime minister, and their political programme, before any general election.A party or coalition which emerges with the largest share of the votes - provided this exceeds 42% - will be awarded 105 additional seats in parliament (70 in the lower house and 35 in the senate), which could turn a narrow victory into a more comfortable majority.Centre-left members held up signs with slogans including "No to the scam" and "fraudulent law" during a debate ahead of the vote, and accused the government of forcing through the new voting rules."Go ahead and change the electoral law, we will win in any case under any voting system," said Democratic Party (PD) leader Elly Schlein.Five Star leader and former Prime Minister Giuseppe Conte told AFP news agency that the move was "a mess, a convoluted scheme, devised solely to find a formula to gain an advantage in the upcoming elections".The proposals have also exposed tensions within the ranks of Meloni's coalition, too, with the Brothers of Italy (FdI) party and its allies, the far-right League and centre-right Forza Italia.Analysts had predicted that Thursday's final vote was unlikely to fail - particularly given the number of lawmakers who would risk losing their eligibility for a parliamentary pension if their term was ended early as a result of the threatened snap election."To those who hoped to see the centre-right divided," Meloni wrote on social media after the vote, "today we respond with facts: we are united, cohesive, and determined to carry forward the commitments made to citizens."She added: "We are introducing rules designed to promote the stability and parliamentary coherence of any government, regardless of its political colour."Meloni's term officially comes to an end in October 2027, although she could bring elections forward to the spring.

schema.headline: Italy approves elections overhaul as opposition accuse Meloni of 'scam' law

title: Neha Bora: India's feisty Gen Z protester who is taking on Modi
description: When India's Gen Z-led protesters return to Delhi this weekend for demonstrations seeking the resignation of the country's top election official, one
body: When India's Gen Z-led protesters return to Delhi this weekend for demonstrations seeking the resignation of the country's top election official, one of the prominent faces at the forefront will be that of a 29-year-old PhD student.Neha Bora is a theatre artist and activist who has been with the All India Students' Association (Aisa), a Left-wing organisation known for campus politics, for the past decade and been its president for the past two years.But Neha's - who uses "they" and "them" as personal pronouns - visibility is no longer limited to campuses.Viral videos over the past few days show them being dragged through the street by a group of female police officials, climbing on top of police barricades, raising their fist and shouting slogans, and being detained.Photos of them smiling while being carried away by policewomen have also gone viral.In a recent BBC Bangla interview, external, Neha played down the attention they've been receiving."I know it happened in front of the camera so it seems like it's something different," they said. "But I have seen all student activists with the Left doing the same things that I have been doing. It's just that there is a camera on me, so people think something different is happening."The attention on Neha comes at a time when several high-profile protests are being held on India's streets in what is being seen as one of the biggest challenges to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's 12 years in power.There's the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - a Gen Z-led online satirical movement - that held weeks-long protests in Delhi in the summer over education reforms. It ended in July only after education minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation.Separately, some of India's opposition parties, especially the Congress, have also taken to the streets over electoral reforms. For the past few days, videos of Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra being shoved and jostled and detained have gone viral and made headlines in India.Saturday's protest in Delhi has been called by the CJP, which is seeking the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating electoral rolls to favour Modi's BJP. Both the Election Commission and the BJP have rejected the accusation.Although not a member of the CJP, Neha has said their group would also participate. Born in the northern state of Uttarakhand, Neha lived in different cities as a child as their army officer father moved for his postings. After graduating from Delhi University, they did a master's degree from Ambedkar University in the capital and are now a PhD student at the prestigious Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU).Neha first came into the spotlight in the summer during the CJP's protest over education reforms.Neha and Aisa were at the protest from the start, but not many knew them at that point. That changed after 28 June, when educationist and scientist Sonam Wangchuk began a hunger strike in CJP's support and Neha and a few others from Aisa also joined him."It was an obvious choice for us. We've been protesting against paper leaks and education reforms for a long time," Neha later said in an interview.While most of the attention was focused on Wangchuk, whose reputation and presence galvanised the movement, Neha's outspokenness and combative speeches began to get them noticed.After Wangchuk and others were moved to hospital, Neha continued fasting despite having lost 8kg. Even after being moved to hospital, they said in a video: "The fight continues. Once I've recovered, we'll meet you again on the streets to continue our fight for our right."After the protests ended in July, Neha has established themselves as a Gen Z leader who's courted by the CJP and media, besides appearing alongside Rahul Gandhi at press conferences.But Neha's involvement with Aisa and leftist politics and statements criticising PM Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah and other BJP leaders have also led to "lots of disagreements with my family as my parents are staunch supporters of BJP".And last month, at least three police complaints were lodged, external in Uttar Pradesh state by BJP against Neha for making "objectionable remarks" against the chief minister - they came two days after Aisa's police complaint that Neha had received death threats, external.Neha, who has been travelling to many Indian cities to participate in protests in support of students, also made headlines when a man allegedly threw ink, external at them during a protest march in Jharkhand state. A photo Neha shared on Instagram showed their face streaked with ink stains. Police said they had detained the man. The noisy protests and repeated detentions have earned Neha a reputation for being a street fighter."The streets have always dictated the course of politics in this country and they will continue to do so, more so in the coming few years," they told BBC Bangla."If we look at the social changes of the recent past, those social changes did not come from people sitting in parliament; they came from the streets," they said.Now as the authorities gear up for 10 October's protest at Jantar Mantar against CEC Kumar, Neha and Aisa have said they would be back in the streets with the CJP  to "protect democracy".

schema.headline: Neha Bora: India's feisty Gen Z protester who is taking on Modi

title: Anne Carson: 'Bold and inventive' Canadian poet wins Nobel Prize in Literature
description: Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson has been awarded this year's Nobel Prize in Literature.Carson, 76, is celebrated for works that oft
body: Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson has been awarded this year's Nobel Prize in Literature.Carson, 76, is celebrated for works that often cross the boundaries between poetry, fiction and scholarship.The Nobel Prize committee said they had selected her "for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature".Carson responded by joking that the judges were "crazy" for honouring her. "I think they're all crazy... Well, you know, it's crazy," she told public broadcaster RUV in Iceland, where she is currently staying.The Nobel Prize is awarded for a lifetime's body of work and is regarded as the most prestigious award in global literature, with the winner receiving 12 million Swedish kronor (£900,000, $1.2m).Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, said she had broken the news to Carson on the phone shortly before the public announcement. "She had time to tell me was that she is, for the moment, in Iceland, where she is listening to the wind," Carlberg, said."She was taken by surprise but very happy. I could hear that in her voice."

schema.headline: Anne Carson: 'Bold and inventive' Canadian poet wins Nobel Prize in Literature

title: Crazy Rich Asians TV show to reunite Constance Wu and Henry Golding
description: Four of the stars of 2018's Crazy Rich Asians film are reprising their roles for a TV show of the same name. The series will pick up events after the
body: Four of the stars of 2018's Crazy Rich Asians film are reprising their roles for a TV show of the same name. The series will pick up events after the end of the hit film, with Constance Wu and Henry Golding playing their lead roles of Rachel and Nick, while Ronny Chieng is back as Eddie and Oscar winner Michelle Yeoh will have a recurring role as Nick's mother Eleanor. "It's a 'Crazy Rich' family reunion!" said Adele Lim, who co-wrote the film, calling it the sequel we've been waiting for". It will "delve into the characters and worlds of Kevin Kwan's brilliant books" over eight episodes, she said.The show will be made by HBO, and the news was announced days after HBO's parent company Warner Bros announced its £110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Paramount Skydance. Adapted from Kwan's bestseller books, written between 2013 and 2017, the film topped the US box office and was nominated for two Golden Globes.It featured an all-Asian cast and told the story of an Asian-American woman who gets a culture shock meeting her boyfriend's ultra-wealthy family in Singapore.Lim is showrunner for the new TV series and will be one of the executive producers, as will the the film's director Jon M Chu.

schema.headline: Crazy Rich Asians TV show to reunite Constance Wu and Henry Golding

title: Saudi Arabia says three nationals killed in Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport.
description: Three Saudi nationals have been killed in two attacks on the international airport in the capital, Riyadh, the country's civil aviation authority has
body: Three Saudi nationals have been killed in two attacks on the international airport in the capital, Riyadh, the country's civil aviation authority has said after Yemen's Houthis said they targeted the facility.The attacks also resulted in "injuries to a number of Saudi citizens and residents of various nationalities", the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement on X.It said the first attack on Thursday targeted the airport while the second one struck an aircraft belonging to state carrier Saudia.One of its pilots was among those killed, the airline said in a statement.Air traffic had returned to normal, the civil aviation authority said.Yemen's Houthi group said on Thursday it had attacked the airport with two missiles, reports said.The Iran-aligned group said it had also targeted an airport in Najran city near the Saudi border with Yemen, and Khamis Mushait air base further north. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed these attacks.The latest casualties follow the deaths of three people in Houthi attacks on two Saudi airports on October 6 and 7.Two were killed and 28 wounded in an attack at Abha International Airport, the civil aviation body said on Wednesday. Another person was killed at King Khalid airport.The latest attacks come amid mark an escalation in renewed fighting between Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthis, who control most of the country's north-west.The Houthi military spokesperson said the previous two attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports were in "response to the Saudi aggression against our country" which saw "60 airstrikes and missile attacks in the past 24 hours".The group says it is targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war.The conflict has worsened in recent weeks, after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive.That included the port of Mokha on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is the narrowest point of the Red Sea and a chokepoint for global shipping.But Yemeni pro-government forces have since said they had "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea.A Saudi-led coalition was formed in 2015 after Arab countries joined forces to stop the Houthis taking over Yemen from the country's internationally recognised government.A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022 after years of air strikes and ground fighting led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, triggering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.But the informal ceasefire began to unravel in July.The Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. They said they were retaliating for what they say is a years-long Saudi blockade, and for an air strike on Sanaa airport.

schema.headline: Saudi Arabia says three nationals killed in Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport.

title: Starlink: Why Elon Musk is taking on Mukesh Ambani and Jio over satellite internet
description: Elon Musk has questioned whether billionaire Mukesh Ambani is the "real boss of India" as his satellite internet company Starlink struggles to secure
body: Elon Musk has questioned whether billionaire Mukesh Ambani is the "real boss of India" as his satellite internet company Starlink struggles to secure final approval to launch in the country.The remark came a day after Musk accused unnamed powerful business interests of trying to block Starlink's entry into India. He then singled out Ambani, whose Reliance conglomerate owns Jio, India's biggest mobile network operator.India has rejected Musk's allegations, saying its satellite communications rules are fair and non-discriminatory.Ambani and Reliance Group have not responded to Musk's remarks. The BBC has reached out to them for commentThe row comes as competition grows in India's satellite internet market, with Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel also preparing to launch services.The rivalry is complicated by the fact that Starlink has also partnered with Ambani's Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel. In March 2025, both companies signed agreements with SpaceX to distribute Starlink equipment and services in India, subject to government approval. The companies also said they could explore sharing network infrastructure. The BBC has also reached out to Bharti Airtel for comment. Musk first made the allegations on Wednesday, accusing "certain oligarchs" of maintaining a "monopolistic chokehold" on Indian consumers."You can guess who they are," he wrote on X, external, adding that blocking Starlink was "a crime against the people of India".On Thursday, India's Ministry of Communications responded, saying that three operators - Starlink, Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio Satellite Communications - were at broadly the same stage of the approval process, with all three awaiting security clearances and spectrum allocation before they can launch commercial services."The suggestion that the framework or its application is unfair or discriminatory is baseless and misconceived," the ministry said, without naming Musk directly.Musk continued to question the delay, saying Starlink was already licensed in more than 165 countries."Starlink is licensed in over 165 countries and has spent five years complying with every single law and requirement of the government of India, so why still no license? Is Ambani the real boss of India?" he wrote on X on Thursday.Starlink, owned by Musk's SpaceX, uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas where mobile networks and broadband cables are difficult or expensive to install.The company has been trying to enter India since 2021 and has secured key licences. But it still needs final security clearances and spectrum allocation before it can begin commercial services.Wednesday's row unfolded as senior executives from Starlink, Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel gathered at the India Mobile Congress in Delhi, where all three companies discussed their plans for satellite internet services.Speaking at the event, Akash Ambani, chairman of Reliance Jio Infocomm and Mukesh Ambani's son, said the company was developing its own satellite communications technology and working towards regulatory approvals.Asked by a reporter about Musk's allegations, Akash declined to comment and only said, "We want to be heads down and deliver value to our Indian consumers."    Bharti Airtel chairman Sunil Bharti Mittal said his company's satellite venture was also awaiting government approvals.SpaceX executive Lauren Dreyer, who oversees Starlink's business operations, said the company had spent years working with Indian regulators and had built security controls into its network to meet the country's requirements.Security has been a key concern surrounding Starlink's entry into India. In 2024, Indian authorities said they had recovered Starlink equipment during a drug-smuggling investigation in the remote Andaman and Nicobar Islands and an army operation in the northeastern state of Manipur.Musk said at that time that Starlink's service had never been active in India, arguing that the equipment recovered by authorities could not have been using its satellite network.Questions also remain over how affordable the service would be for Indian consumers, particularly those in rural areas.India is one of the world's largest internet markets but access remains uneven, particularly in remote areas where mobile networks and broadband cables are difficult or expensive to build.Musk has argued that Starlink could help bridge this gap. "Starlink in India would enable high-speed, affordable internet connectivity for those who can't afford current prices or who don't have a connection at all!" he wrote on X on Wednesday. The company has yet to announce prices for India, but some experts say its plans elsewhere suggest the service could be beyond the reach of many Indian households.In the US, Starlink's residential plans start at $55 a month, although prices and equipment costs vary by plan and location.

schema.headline: Starlink: Why Elon Musk is taking on Mukesh Ambani and Jio over satellite internet

title: Christa Pike's health has seen 'profound turnaround' in last three days, lawyers say
description: Christa Pike has 'profound' health turnaround after botched execution, lawyers sayFigure caption, Watch: What we know about Christa Pike's "shock" rec
body: Christa Pike has 'profound' health turnaround after botched execution, lawyers sayFigure caption, Watch: What we know about Christa Pike's "shock" recovery in hospitalByNardine SaadChrista Pike has made a "profound" turnaround after last week's botched attempt to execute her in the US state of Tennessee, her lawyers say.Pike, 50, was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995. She survived two injections of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September and was taken to hospital in a critical condition.In a statement on Thursday, Pike's lawyers described her recovery as "remarkable" and said she is able to walk with assistance and is eating. She has also regained some movement in her arms, which were badly injured during the attempted execution, they said."Physicians are encouraged by her physical recovery," the statement said.The case is now in uncharted territory as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.Image source, Reuters"Christa is dealing with the profound psychological trauma of having survived a failed execution, including the terror, pain and uncertainty of believing she was about to die," her legal team said. Pike's lawyers said they do not know the full emotional and psychological toll of the execution attempt or how long it will take her to recover.They added that while she struggles to process what happened, she "continues to express concern for others, particularly the family of her victim Colleen Slemmer".Slemmer's mother, who was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death, has branded the failed execution a "mess".Pike's boyfriend at the time of Slemmer's murder, Tadaryl Shipp, was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison.Pike was 18 and Shipp was 17 when they beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.A court has ordered officials to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution, which could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.On Wednesday, Judge I'Ashea Myles ordered that "anything that was in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained," including IV lines and syringes, as well as waste, such as packaging, inserts and labels.The judge also demanded documentation on Pike's psychological condition before, during and after the failed execution.She advised the state to take "special care" not to misplace or accidentally delete any information that may be pertinent to the case.Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered a pause on all executions for the rest of the year and said he wants answers about what went wrong.Pike's lawyers have called on the governor to downgrade Pike's punishment to life in prison without parole.Proponents of capital punishment have suggested using a different method to put her to death.Killing Death RowCould the US death penalty ever die out? A surreal story about a man in Acton, London, who supplied the USA with lethal drugs tips Livvy Haydock into the macabre world of Death Row.

schema.headline: Christa Pike's health has seen 'profound turnaround' in last three days, lawyers say

title: South African anti-migrant protests: Cars torched and shops looted in Durban and Soweto
description: At least 24 vehicles have been set ablaze and foreign-owned shops looted in South Africa as anti-immigration protests descended into violence in two m
body: At least 24 vehicles have been set ablaze and foreign-owned shops looted in South Africa as anti-immigration protests descended into violence in two major cities, police say. Unrest broke out on Thursday in Soweto, a sprawling township outside Johannesburg, the country's largest city, and Durban, a major port on the east coast.The violence comes amid growing anger over a court ruling which would allow some migrants who had arrived in the country illegally to apply for asylum.This had led to long queues outside immigration centres and the government on Friday said it would change the way it would comply with that ruling, without giving details.The Department of Home Affairs said the current policy had seen its staff "overwhelmed", while "serious threats to public safety and order had emerged".It said that the new policy would still abide by the Constitutional Court ruling.South Africa has experienced repeated outbreaks of xenophobic violence, often targeting migrants from neighbouring countries.Thursday's demonstration turned violent following allegations that a foreign national had assaulted one of the protesters in Durban. Three foreign nationals were arrested in connection with the alleged assault, police said.In Durban, in the eastern province of KwaZulu-Natal, protesters gathered outside a government refugee reception centre demanding that it stop accepting asylum applications.Police fired rubber bullets to disperse crowds as businesses in the city centre shut their doors."There were clashes between foreign nationals in the area and South African nationals," senior local police officer Xolani Fihla told state broadcaster SABC."At the present moment, I can confirm that no injuries have been reported," he added.Police said 14 vehicles were torched in Durban and 10 in Soweto, where gunshots were also reported during confrontations between residents and foreign shopkeepers.Acting national police commissioner Lt Gen Puleng Dimpane condemned the destruction of property.In Orlando West, a neighbourhood of Soweto, residents had initially gathered to demand the closure of small convenience stores, known locally as spaza shops, operated by foreign nationals.Protesters forced foreign traders out of some areas, while shops were attacked and a building was set on fire, local media reported. Police said reinforcements had been deployed to prevent further violence.The authorities have promised to pursue those responsible for the destruction.The latest unrest follows a July ruling by Constitutional Court, South Africa's highest court, which struck down restrictions preventing some people from seeking asylum because of how they entered the country or missed immigration deadlines.The judgment means asylum seekers must be allowed to submit applications, even if they entered South Africa without the required documents.This prompted hundreds of people to gather at refugee reception centres, fuelling anger among anti-immigration campaigners who fear the decision will encourage undocumented migration.Government spokesman William Baloyi told Reuters news agency that people had deliberately spread false claims about the judgment, creating the impression that undocumented migrants would automatically be granted legal status.Baloyi insisted that the ruling does not automatically give migrants refugee status or the right to remain permanently in South Africa.Officials say applications will still be assessed individually and applicants will remain subject to immigration checks.Earlier this year, anti-immigration groups staged weeks of demonstrations demanding that undocumented foreign nationals leave the country by 30 June.The protests forced tens of thousands of migrants to flee, with some returning home through repatriation programmes organised by their governments.South Africa has struggled with xenophobic attacks for nearly two decades. In 2008, more than 60 people were killed and tens of thousands displaced during widespread attacks on foreign nationals.The latest unrest comes against a backdrop of widespread poverty, deep inequality and unemployment affecting roughly a third of the workforce.Migrants are frequently accused of taking jobs, contributing to crime and placing pressure on public services, although researchers say such sweeping claims are not supported by evidence.Despite its economic difficulties, South Africa remains one of the continent's main destinations for migrants seeking employment, safety and better opportunities.Additional reporting by Christian Parkinson in Johannesburg

schema.headline: South African anti-migrant protests: Cars torched and shops looted in Durban and Soweto

title: Residents airlifted to safety in central Chile as El Niño blamed for torrential rains
description: Police in central Chile have airlifted several residents to safety after rising floodwaters left them trapped in their homes.Recent torrential rains c
body: Police in central Chile have airlifted several residents to safety after rising floodwaters left them trapped in their homes.Recent torrential rains caused the Mapocho river to burst its banks, flooding large parts of the city of Talagante, 35km (22 miles) south-west of the capital, Santiago.Santiago has seen 74mm of rainfall in the first seven days of this month, making it the rainiest October for the area in 76 years, meteorologists have said.They have warned that this year's unusually strong El Niño climate phenomenon will likely continue to bring unusually wet weather, powerful winds and storms to the region during the southern hemisphere's spring.Officials said one person had been found dead in a flooded underpass in the city of San Bernardo, south of Santiago, although they have yet to confirm the cause of death. In Talagante, police used helicopters to rescue people and pets living on the banks of the Mapocho who had been surprised by the fast-rising waters overnight.Dirt roads turned into rivers in the riverside community which, unlike in July's storms, had not been evacuated ahead of the heavy downpours.

schema.headline: Residents airlifted to safety in central Chile as El Niño blamed for torrential rains

title: Fired OpenAI researchers say they were let go for 'prioritising safety'
description: Three former OpenAI researchers sacked for allegedly mishandling information claim they were instead let go because they raised safety concerns at the
body: Three former OpenAI researchers sacked for allegedly mishandling information claim they were instead let go because they raised safety concerns at the tech firm."I believe we were fired for prioritising safety over the near-term interests of OpenAI as a corporation," Mikita Balesni posted on X, external alongside an open letter to the ChatGPT-maker, written with fellow ex-employees.On 2 October, a spokesperson for the AI firm told the BBC its investigation "confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures".OpenAI repeated these claims, external on Friday morning in a note from research leaders."We want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out," the note said. "Our internal investigation uncovered a significant breach of trust beyond what's outlined in the letter they published and we stand by the decision to not continue their employment."The dismissals come amid a growing debate over AI safety and the potential risks advanced AI systems could pose to society.The joint letter to OpenAI leadership was written by Balesni, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang, who say they were all, until recently, safety or alignment employees at the company.Alignment is the practice of building human ethical ideas and principles into the technology. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value.The former staff members raised concerns that their firings had made employees at the tech company "afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI".Reposting the letter, Korbak wrote, external: "For months, I'd been raising safety concerns that we're losing the ability to monitor what AI agents think, one of our best tools for catching when they misbehave. "I believe that was why I was fired."OpenAI said it was finalising contracts with third-party safety assessors and would announce details in the coming weeks."We were not the first to be pushed out of OpenAI under suspicious circumstances," Wang said in a post on X, external."Unless the employees take a stand now against this kind of manoeuvre, I am concerned we will not be the last."

schema.headline: Fired OpenAI researchers say they were let go for 'prioritising safety'

title: US deportations to African countries unlawful and exploit suffering - HRW
description: Campaign group Human Rights Watch (HRW) says the deportation of migrants from the US to third-party African countries is against the law and exploits
body: Campaign group Human Rights Watch (HRW) says the deportation of migrants from the US to third-party African countries is against the law and exploits suffering to deter migration."Many, if not most" of the deportees have no practical option but to return to their home countries regardless of the harm they face there, HRW says in a report.Since Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025, more than 500 people have been sent to African countries where they are not citizens, the group says, citing US data.The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said "third country removals are an essential public safety tool that remove the most dangerous criminal illegal aliens from our streets".Tackling immigration was one of Trump's key pledges during the 2024 election.Eswatini, which welcomed 32 deportees from the US, says three people - from Yemen, Belize and Laos - "voluntarily departed" to their home countries recently.According to HRW, some of the countries accepting the deportees have "arbitrarily detained" or sent them to their home countries, where they face "the risk of persecution or torture".The group said that people sent to Eswatini, Ghana and South Sudan, had been arbitrarily detained and faced ill-treatment while in detention.In Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea and Ghana, the deportees had been sent to their countries of origin despite the risk of "violating the principle of nonrefoulement [that people should not be sent to a country where they face torture, cruel treatment, or threats to their life and freedom]", it said.The group cited an unnamed US official as having told a Senate hearing that the point for the administration was that it could "threaten people that they will literally be dropped in the middle of nowhere"."The point is to scare people," HRW said."Deporting people to countries where they have never set foot is part of a US policy designed to cause human suffering as a means to deter migration," said Michael Garcia Bochenek, the group's interim US programme director.In a statement from to the BBC, DHS said: "ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] is given diplomatic assurances from destination countries that the illegal aliens being removed there will be safe. When an individual is no longer in ICE custody, ICE is no longer responsible for them."White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told the BBC that those being sent to third countries were those whose home nations refused to take them or who had court orders preventing them being sent home."Any illegal alien who wants to go home, we will arrange a free flight for them and give them a $3,000 check," she said.None of the African countries named has commented on the report. However, while announcing the recent departure of three migrants on Wednesday, Eswatini said that it was committed to ensuring that the "rights, dignity and well-being of third-country nationals were respected and protected".HRW said it interviewed 24 third-country nationals in six countries - Cameroon, Central African Republic, Democratic Republic of Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Eswatini and South Sudan.Some described to the group "abusive treatment" during their deportation flights, including being chained for about 18 hours and with no knowledge of their destination. They were also "denied access to essential medication, and often did not receive sufficient food or water"."The opaque deals that facilitate these transfers, some of which are still secret, are part of a US policy that violates international human rights law," HRW says.According to the report, at least a dozen people who identified as lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender (LGBT) were sent to African states that criminalise same-sex relations.Among them were refugees granted protection in the US based on the likelihood they would be persecuted back home because of their orientation or gender identity.In November, a Nigerian man deported from the US initially to Ghana expressed his fears to the BBC after he and five others were secretly transferred to Togo.He spoke of his fears about returning to Nigeria, where his association with a separatist activist group could lead to his arrest and torture.In DR Congo, HRW says it was told by a US lawyer that of the 15 people from Colombia, Peru and Ecuador deported to the country in April, none remained there by late September, with 11 having returned to their home countries."The uncertainty and other conditions they faced in the Democratic Republic of Congo call into question whether these returns to countries of origin were voluntary," the group said.Equatorial Guinea, which received 65 people, quickly sent at least two people to their home countries, HRW said.Burundi announced late last month that it had agreed to take in migrants deported from the US.

schema.headline: US deportations to African countries unlawful and exploit suffering - HRW

title: Nana Patekar: Outspoken Indian actor Nana Patekar dies suddenly at 75
description: Veteran Indian actor Nana Patekar, known for his intense, fiery performances on stage and in film, has died at the age of 75 in Goa.One of the most re
body: Veteran Indian actor Nana Patekar, known for his intense, fiery performances on stage and in film, has died at the age of 75 in Goa.One of the most recognisable faces of Indian cinema, Patekar won three National Film Awards and became known for playing difficult and often volatile characters. He was also a prominent figure in Marathi language cinema and theatre.He was admitted to a hospital after being found unconscious at his home in Goa in the early hours of Thursday."Despite 45 minutes of continuous CPR, he could not be revived," Dr Shekhar Salkar of Manipal Hospital in Goa told ANI news agency. Tributes have poured in from actors and politicians across India.Dr Salkar later told PTI news agency that the hospital team found Patekar at his home "unconscious and almost unresponsive".The team continued giving him CPR even while taking him to the hospital, located about 10 minutes away, but he was dead by the time they reached there, he added. Dr Salkar said Patekar had suffered a cardiac arrest, but it was not clear what had triggered it.Family, friends and fans paid their last respects to the actor at Goa Medical College, ahead of his funeral which was to take place later in the day with full state honours at his farm house in the western city of Pune in Maharashtra state. In the evening, his remains were flown to Pune by air ambulance, where the state's chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis paid his last respects, before Patekar's body was taken to his farm in Donje village where last rites were performed and he was cremated.Times of India reports that his son, Malhar, told reporters afterwards that his father has not truly gone anywhere and will to remain with them - even if not physically - and his commitment to social welfare would live on.Earlier, Prime Minister Narendra Modi led tributes to the actor, praising Patekar's versatility and outspoken personality.Patekar portrayed characters that would "remain etched in the memory of generations", Modi wrote on X, adding that his death had left "a vast void in the artistic world".Bollywood veteran Anupam Kher paid tribute to his friend on social media, saying he would miss his warmth and extraordinary performances and called him "one of the finest actors and human beings in Indian cinema".Another Bollywood star Shah Rukh Khan called him "a mentor, a teacher, a critic and a friend", adding that Patekar has "left a void not only in the world of cinema but in the hearts of all Indians and the world".Akshay Kumar, who appeared alongside Patekar in the comedy film Welcome, remembered him as a rare performer whose voice, intensity and honesty could command an audience's attention. Patekar made his debut with the film Gaman in 1978 and continued to play smaller roles in several films. But the intensity that he brought on the screen was hard to miss and soon he landed a role in Parinda in 1989, making him a household name across India. He won his first National Film Award and the Filmfare Award as well for his portrayal of the gangster Anna in the film. He didn't look back after this and portrayed many memorable roles in films in the 1990s. The range of characters he played showcased the depth of his acting talent and mastery of his craft. Famous  dialogues from his films, delivered in his inimitable rasping voice, were quoted in school corridors and tea stalls. Many professional comedians imitate his distinctive style even today."He had a distinctive style of working and how he approached characters. As a person, he was outspoken and difficult to get along with but directors would still want to work with him because he was simply a fantastic actor," film trade analyst Komal Nahta told BBC.His portrayal of Major Chauhan in Prahaar – a film he also directed – won him praise. His other characters, including the patriotic hero of Tirangaa and Pratap Narayan Tilak in Krantiveer, also won him accolades.Just when critics thought that playing loud characters was his mainstay, he proved them wrong by delivering a mesmerising performance in Khamoshi as a person who could not hear or speak.Director Prakash Jha's Rajneeti in 2010 added another dimension to his acting as his portrayal of an astute politician was delivered with perfection.The breadth of Patekar's career showcases the wide range of his work. He played different but contrasting roles like that of a notorious gangster or a policeman with equal ease. He also sometimes worked behind the camera as a director and writer.His three national awards for Parinda, Krantiveer and Agni Sakshi are testament to his wide-ranging career.Patekar was an influential figure too in both Marathi and Hindi theatre. Before making his debut in films, he was involved in theatre, where he developed his gritty style of dialogue delivery and also mastered the intensity he brought to his on-screen characters. Purush and Hamidabai Chi Kothi were two of his most famous plays. Despite being successful in films, he remained active in theatre throughout his professional life.Patekar was known for his activism and didn't mince his words while criticising the government of the day. He was direct, and almost brazen and unapologetic, when it came to criticising ministers and their policies - and did so quite publicly.Issues related to farmers were particularly close to his heart.His work went beyond just giving statements. In 2015 he and actor Makarand Anaspure established the Naam Foundation, which has worked on farmer welfare and water conservation in Maharashtra.But his career was not without controversies.In 2018, allegations of sexual harassment made by actor Tanushree Dutta against Patekar over an alleged incident on a film set a decade earlier helped spark India's #MeToo movement. Patekar denied the allegations. In 2019, he was cleared of the charges after police said they had not found sufficient evidence against him.Additional reporting by Rachita Prasad

title: Tanker hit by multiple projectiles in Gulf off Qatar, UKMTO says
description: A tanker has been struck by "multiple projectiles" north of Qatar in the Gulf, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency.The in
body: A tanker has been struck by "multiple projectiles" north of Qatar in the Gulf, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency.The incident - a rare attack deep inside the Gulf - happened 51 nautical miles (94km) from Madinat al-Shamal with casualties reported, the UKMTO said.Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard identified the vessel as the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged oil and chemical tanker Acers. On Saturday it was reported as sailing towards the Strait of Hormuz waterway, which connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman.Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the region since the US and Israel's war with Iran began in February.At least 24 seafarers have been killed in 93 confirmed incidents, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization (IMO).The IMO said the last incident that resulted in casualties was on 9 September, when two sailors were killed in an attack on the Panama-flagged tanker El Gaia in the Strait of Hormuz, just north of Oman's Musandam peninsula.This is also the first reported attack on a ship this far west of the Strait of Hormuz since that same day, according to Martin Kelly, head of advisory at EOS Risk Group.Also on Thursday, Vanguard amended an earlier report that had said there was a fire on board another tanker in the Gulf of Oman, about 40km east of Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates. The company clarified that there were no indications a fire occurred on the vessel, which it had identified as the Marshall Islands-flagged Dhalkut.The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Tehran's missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and targeted vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.Over the past two weeks, crude exports through the waterway have averaged 12 million barrels per day (bpd), which is around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts from shipping data company Kpler.

title: Fort Hood survivor supports gunman's execution by firing squad but questions livestream
description: A former US Army sergeant who survived the mass shooting on Fort Hood has said that while he supports the execution of the gunman by firing squad, he
body: A former US Army sergeant who survived the mass shooting on Fort Hood has said that while he supports the execution of the gunman by firing squad, he is concerned about it being livestreamed.Alonzo Lunsford, who was shot seven times, told the BBC that the "method is befitting" for Nidal Hasan because other methods like lethal injection would be "doing him a favour".Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist, fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers in a medical building at Fort Hood, in Texas, in 2009. But while Lunsford agreed with the method of execution, he said it was "not something you should view for entertainment purposes".Speaking to Radio 4's Today programme on Friday, he said: "To show the whole thing without it being censored for the general public, for me personally, I don't agree with that, but it's not about my personal belief."US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the public will be able to view a livestream of the execution, saying it is important for people to see the consequences of this kind of crime. If it goes ahead, and legal experts told the BBC it might not ever happen, it would be the first public execution in the US in almost a century.Lunsford explained that while he is concerned about the "effect" and "message" a livestream would send to younger people, when it comes to the survivors, their families and the families of the victims, they "should be able to look at it"."I'm gonna be there [to watch in person] and before they pull the trigger, I want him to look at me in my eyes and I look at him in his eyes and I want him to know: 'Dude you failed, I'm still here,'" he said."I don't really have any sympathy for him as far as firing squad vs lethal injection, hanging or gas chamber, because he didn't have that same compassion when he did the deed on 5 November," the former sergeant explained. "I think the method is befitting for him because the lethal injection - that's doing him a favour. Gas chamber? Is doing him a favour."But Lunsford said that as a Christian, he has forgiven Hasan because "I cannot heal if I don't forgive him"."We're taught that with your last breath you can ask for forgiveness and I think that's what he [Hasan] should do," he added.Telling his account of what happened that day, he said Hasan got out of his chair and jumped onto a counter, before pulling out a weapon and discharging rounds.Lunford said he was looking for an exit via the back door, which was "two or three strides" away from him when he was first shot above his left eye and then "hit two more times in my back" as he crawled behind a desk."At that point I played dead," he said. When Hasan moved on, he grabbed a nearby wounded soldier and went outside, where Lunsford said Hasan came up behind them and shot him again.One memory he said that "bothers" him from the day was of a woman who told Hasan she was pregnant."We heard a gunshot and the last thing that girl was saying was: 'Oh my god, my baby, my baby.'"Lunsford said personnel don't carry weapons in medical facilities, and that Hasan "took the coward's way out" to attack them there."And then for him to say he is fighting for his cause? I've read the Quran, and everything that he said he was doing that was in the Quran is not supported by the Quran," he explained.Hasan's execution was announced by the Pentagon earlier this week, in what will be the first military execution in more than 60 years.Legal experts have told the BBC there are a number of hurdles around the livestreaming of this which could mean it is successfully challenged in court.Some politicians have been vocal in their opposition.Democratic Senator Chris Murphy told CNN it was "disgusting" while Republican Senator Thom Tillis said public executions were what "oppressive dictators" did."It should not be happening in America," he added in a post on X., external

title: Venezuela's ex-leader Nicolás Maduro charged with conspiracy to commit torture
description: Prosecutors in the United States have accused Venezuela's former leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, of conspiracy to commit torture. Th
body: Prosecutors in the United States have accused Venezuela's former leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, of conspiracy to commit torture. The fresh charges against the couple were made public on Thursday and are in addition to the drug-trafficking and weapons charges already brought against them, which they have denied. Maduro, 63, and Flores, 69, have been in custody since January in a detention centre in Brooklyn, where they were taken after US forces seized them in a pre-dawn raid on their compound in the Venezuelan capital, Caracas. Barry J Pollack, Maduro's attorney, said his client denies the new charges and looks forward to his day in court.Federal prosecutors also announced on Thursday that Flores was added to the earlier narco-terrorism charge.The trial for both Maduro and Flores is set to begin in June 2027. Both are being held in a detention centre in Brooklyn and are expected to remain there after Flores's request to be moved to house arrest was denied by a judge on Thursday.The new accusations relate to the alleged torture of US citizens who were being held in Venezuela while Maduro was in power.The superseding indictment unsealed on Thursday accuses the former presidential couple of "entrenching themselves in power" by presiding "over a system of repression that relied on violence against political opposition, arbitrary detention, and the torture of detainees, including United States citizens". According to the indictment, the torture included "electric shock, asphyxiation, rape, forced nudity, prolonged isolation, starvation, punishment cells, and psychological torture".The prosecutors allege that the psychological torture included threats to kill victims' families, including children. "All of this was done to ensure that  Maduro and Flores retained their power," prosecutors said outside the courthouse on Thursday. "This conduct, we allege, has caused significant harm to Americans, to US citizens", prosecutors said, calling it "the epitome of corruption".The prosecution accuses Flores of having played a key role in the development of the repressive system, ordering that individuals be tortured and even receiving updates on the torture of specific prisoners.The court document alleges that she did so in order to protect members of her family who were involved in illegal activities. The allegations contained in the superseding indictment echo many of the accusations long made by prisoners who have been released from detention in Venezuela.Javier Tarazona, the head of a human rights group in Venezuela, told BBC Mundo's Norberto Paredes earlier this year how he and his brother were held in a tiny punishment cell for 46 days after being arbitrarily arrested. Another former inmate, Ángel Godoy, told BBC Mundo that he was kept isolated for  months and not allowed to contact his wife, who was in turn kept in the dark about his whereabouts. The allegations listed in the superseding indictment made public on Thursday relate to cases during Maduro's time in power.After his ouster, his vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, was sworn in as interim leader with the backing of the Trump administration.While hundreds of political prisoners have been released under an amnesty law since she has taken over power, more than 300 still remain behind bars, according to prisoners' rights group Foro Penal.The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk has warned that his office has received reports alleging that detainees continue to be tortured even after the seizure of Maduro. Türk said in March that "structural and systemic human rights concerns" had persisted in Venezuela despite Maduro's ousting.Venezuela's foreign minister at the time accused Türk of parroting the agenda of "extremists" by citing the allegations.

schema.headline: Venezuela's ex-leader Nicolás Maduro charged with conspiracy to commit torture
